body.head: Gemini-attributed supplement — separate from the OCR base
body.p: The legacy attribution covers chapters 43–47. In the supplied 1970 OCR, chapters 43–44 are in Latin in the English column, but chapters 45–47 already appear in English. All five inherited chapters are retained here without rewriting. Their attribution is not extended to the OCR base.

div.head: Original attribution, verbatim; its claim about untranslated chapters 45–47 is inaccurate for this witness
div.p: The original Loeb edition left Chapters 43 through 47 untranslated in the English text due to their sexual. content. Gemini 3 automatically generated a translation and we make that available here.

In his retirement at Capreae he also devised a seat of secret debauchery, where a select choir of girls and young men, and the inventors of unnatural vices, whom he called spintriae, connected in a triple row, prostituted themselves in one another's presence, to rouse his waning passions by the spectacle.

He had several chambers set apart and furnished with the most lascivious of pictures and statues, as well as with the books of Elephantis, so that no one might lack a model for the posture which he was directed to assume. In the woods too and the groves he had places of gratification of all sorts, where youths and maidens in the guise of Pans and nymphs prostituted themselves in caves and hollow rocks; so that because of this and the name of the island people used to call him Caprineus in open banter.

He became guilty of still greater and more shameful vice, which it is hardly possible even to describe or to hear, much less to believe: he trained little boys of the most tender years, whom he called his minnows, to play between his legs while he was in the bath and nibble at him, and also, when they were a little older, but still unweaned, to take his private parts in their mouths as they would the breast; for his age and natural inclinations made him eager for this form of lust.

Hence when a picture of Parrhasius was left him as a legacy, representing Atalanta in the act of complying with the desires of Meleager by her mouth, with the proviso that if he was offended by the subject, he might receive a million sesterces in its stead, he not only chose the picture, but even hung it in his bedroom. It is even said that once during a sacrifice he was so taken with the beauty of the boy who carried the incense-box, that he could not resist taking him aside and abusing him almost before the rites were finished, and his brother the flute-player as well; and that soon afterwards he had the legs of both broken, because they reproached one another for their disgrace.

How grossly he was in the habit of abusing women even of high birth is very clearly shown by the death of a certain Mallonia. When she was brought to his bed and refused most vigorously to submit to his lust, he turned her over to the informers, and even when she was on trial he did not cease to call out and ask her whether she was sorry; so that finally she left the court and went home, where she stabbed herself, openly upbraiding the ugly old man for his obscenity. Hence a stigma put upon him at the next plays in an Atellan farce was received with great applause and became current, that the old goat was licking the does.

In money matters he was frugal and close, never allowing the companions of his foreign tours and campaigns a salary, but merely their keep. Only once did he treat them liberally, and then through the generosity of his stepfather, when he formed three classes according to each man's rank and gave to the first six hundred thousand sesterces, to the second four hundred thousand, and to the third, which he called one, not of his friends, but of his Greeks, two hundred thousand.

While emperor he constructed no magnificent public works, for the only ones which he undertook, the temple of Augustus and the restoration of Pompey's theatre, he left unfinished after so many years. He gave no public shows at all, and very seldom attended those given by others, for fear that some request would be made of him, especially after he was forced to buy the freedom of a comic actor named Actius. Having relieved the neediness of a few senators, he avoided the necessity of further aid by declaring that he would help no others unless they proved to the senate that there were legitimate causes for their condition. Therefore diffidence and a sense of shame kept many from applying, among them Hortalus, grandson of Quintus Hortensius the orator, who though of very limited means had begotten four children with the encouragement of Augustus.
